items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the pairing of A with T (or U in RNA) by two hydrogen bonds and C with G by three hydrogen bonds"?
items.answer: Complementary base pairing
items.markingKey: Complementary base pairing: the pairing of A with T (or U in RNA) by two hydrogen bonds and C with G by three hydrogen bonds.

items.stem: Explain why a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine in DNA.
items.answer: A two-ring purine with a one-ring pyrimidine gives a constant width of the double helix; the hydrogen-bonding patterns are complementary (A–T, C–G).
items.markingKey: A two-ring purine with a one-ring pyrimidine gives a constant width of the double helix [1]; the hydrogen-bonding patterns are complementary (A–T, C–G) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the structure of DNA makes it stable.
items.answer: Sugar–phosphate backbone joined by strong covalent phosphodiester bonds; bases protected inside helix; many hydrogen bonds between base pairs; base stacking.
items.markingKey: any 3 from: Sugar–phosphate backbone joined by strong covalent phosphodiester bonds; bases protected inside helix; many hydrogen bonds between base pairs; base stacking (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule from wheat contains 3,000 base pairs, and 29% of its bases are adenine. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases. (b) Calculate the number of cytosine bases in the molecule.

A double-stranded DNA molecule from yeast contains 1,500 base pairs, and 31% of its bases are adenine. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases. (b) Calculate the number of cytosine bases in the molecule. (c) Calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds between the bases.

An athlete in Colombo uses about 50 kg of ATP per day, but the body contains only about 50 g of ATP at any one time. (a) Explain how the body can use so much ATP with such a small amount present. (b) Explain why ATP rather than glucose is used as the immediate energy source.
items.answer: (a) ATP is continuously hydrolysed to ADP + Pi and regenerated from them by respiration; it is recycled many times a day. (b) Hydrolysis of ATP is one step releasing small usable amounts; glucose release needs many steps and too much energy at once.
items.markingKey: (a) ATP is continuously hydrolysed to ADP + Pi and regenerated from them by respiration [1]; it is recycled many times a day [1] [2] (b) Hydrolysis of ATP is one step releasing small usable amounts [1]; glucose release needs many steps and too much energy at once [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why DNA with a high proportion of C–G pairs needs a higher temperature to separate its strands.
items.answer: C–G pairs have three hydrogen bonds compared with two for A–T, so more energy is needed to break them.
items.markingKey: C–G pairs have three hydrogen bonds compared with two for A–T [1]; so more energy is needed to break them [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) Adenine + ribose (adenosine) + three phosphate groups. (b) Contraction (myosin heads); active transport of Ca²⁺; protein synthesis; glycogen synthesis.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "DNA helicase"?
options: The enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds.
The new strand synthesised continuously in the 5′ to 3′ direction towards the replication fork.
The enzyme that joins free activated nucleotides to form a new strand complementary to the template, working in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
The enzyme that breaks hydrogen bonds between bases to unwind and separate the two strands of DNA.
items.answer: The enzyme that breaks hydrogen bonds between bases to unwind and separate the two strands of DNA.
items.markingKey: DNA helicase: the enzyme that breaks hydrogen bonds between bases to unwind and separate the two strands of DNA.

items.stem: Explain why replication is described as semi-conservative.
items.answer: Each new DNA molecule consists of one original (parental) strand, conserved, and one newly made strand.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Each new DNA molecule consists of one original (parental) strand; conserved; and one newly made strand (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Explain why one strand is copied continuously and the other in fragments.
items.answer: The strands are antiparallel; DNA polymerase works only 5′→3′, so one strand is made continuously towards the fork and the other in short fragments away from it, later joined by ligase.
items.markingKey: any 3 from: The strands are antiparallel; DNA polymerase works only 5′→3′; so one strand is made continuously towards the fork and the other in short fragments away from it; later joined by ligase (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: In an experiment like that of Meselson and Stahl, E. coli was grown for many generations in medium containing ¹⁵N, then transferred to ¹⁴N medium. DNA was extracted and centrifuged after each generation. (a) State the expected percentages of heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N), hybrid and light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N) DNA after 2 generations in ¹⁴N. (b) Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) heavy 0%, hybrid 50%, light 50% (b) Each original ¹⁵N strand is conserved and always pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand, so there are always 2 hybrid molecules per original molecule; all other molecules (2 of 4) are light.
items.markingKey: (a) heavy 0 [1]; hybrid 2 ÷ 4 = 50% [1]; light 50% [1] (b) parental strands conserved [1]; each pairs with new ¹⁴N strand [1] [5]

items.stem: The genome of yeast (many origins) contains 1.2 × 10⁷ base pairs. Each replication fork copies 100 base pairs per second and there are 800 replication forks working at once. (a) Calculate the time to replicate the genome in minutes. (b) Explain why eukaryotic chromosomes have many origins of replication.
items.answer: (a) 2.50 min (b) Eukaryotic DNA is very long; with one origin replication would take far too long, so many origins allow S phase to be completed in a few hours.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.2 × 10⁷ ÷ (100 × 800) = 150 s [1]; ÷ 60 = 2.50 min [1] (b) long DNA [1]; many origins speed replication [1] [4]

items.stem: A student in Nairobi models DNA replication. One strand of a short section of DNA has the base sequence CCTTTCACCCAG. (a) Describe the roles of DNA helicase and DNA polymerase in replicating this section. (b) Explain why both new DNA molecules have the same base sequence.
items.answer: (a) Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds and unwinds the strands; DNA polymerase joins activated nucleotides (complementary to template) by phosphodiester bonds, 5′→3′. items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "DNA ligase"?

The new strand synthesised continuously in the 5′ to 3′ direction towards the replication fork.
DNA replication in which each new molecule contains one strand from the original molecule and one newly synthesised strand.

items.stem: Describe the process of translation.
items.answer: mRNA attaches to ribosome; tRNA with anticodon complementary to start codon brings methionine; second tRNA binds next codon; peptide bond forms between amino acids; ribosome moves along one codon; first tRNA leaves; continues until a stop codon; polypeptide released.

items.stem: Explain how the sickle cell mutation leads to the symptoms of sickle cell anaemia.
items.answer: Substitution in the β-globin gene changes glutamic acid to valine (non-polar); haemoglobin molecules stick together at low oxygen, forming fibres; red cells become sickle-shaped, carry less oxygen and block capillaries.

items.answer: (a) Free nucleotides pair with exposed bases on the template only in the combinations A–T and C–G, so the new strand is complementary to the template and identical to the original partner strand. items.stem: The genome of a human cell (many origins) contains 3.0 × 10⁹ base pairs. Each replication fork copies 100 base pairs per second and there are 30,000 replication forks working at once. (a) Calculate the time to replicate the genome in minutes. (b) Explain why eukaryotic chromosomes have many origins of replication.
items.answer: (a) 16.7 min (b) Eukaryotic DNA is very long; with one origin replication would take far too long, so many origins allow S phase to be completed in a few hours.
items.markingKey: (a) 3.0 × 10⁹ ÷ (100 × 30,000) = 1000 s [1]; ÷ 60 = 16.7 min [1] (b) long DNA [1]; many origins speed replication [1] [4]

items.stem: A student in Lagos models DNA replication. One strand of a short section of DNA has the base sequence AGTGTCTTCCAC. (a) Describe the roles of DNA helicase and DNA polymerase in replicating this section. (b) Explain why the cell needs a supply of activated nucleotides and ATP during replication.
items.answer: (a) Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds and unwinds the strands; DNA polymerase joins activated nucleotides (complementary to template) by phosphodiester bonds, 5′→3′. (b) Nucleotides (with extra phosphates) are the monomers; energy is needed to form phosphodiester bonds / unwind DNA.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "exon"?
options: A coding sequence of a gene that remains in mature mRNA after splicing.
The strand of DNA that is transcribed (read) to make mRNA.
A property of the genetic code in which most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
The production of an mRNA molecule complementary to the template strand of a gene, catalysed by RNA polymerase.
items.answer: A coding sequence of a gene that remains in mature mRNA after splicing.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why an insertion of three bases usually has a smaller effect than an insertion of one base. (b) Explain how the sickle cell mutation leads to the symptoms of sickle cell anaemia.
items.answer: (a) Three bases add one codon (one extra amino acid) without changing the reading frame; one base causes a frameshift, changing all following codons. (b) Substitution in the β-globin gene changes glutamic acid to valine (non-polar); haemoglobin molecules stick together at low oxygen, forming fibres; red cells become sickle-shaped, carry less oxygen and block capillaries.

An athlete in Seoul uses about 70 kg of ATP per day, but the body contains only about 50 g of ATP at any one time. (a) Explain how the body can use so much ATP with such a small amount present. (b) Calculate how many times each ATP molecule is recycled per day, on average. (c) Give three uses of ATP in muscle cells.
items.answer: (a) ATP is continuously hydrolysed to ADP + Pi and regenerated from them by respiration; it is recycled many times a day. (b) 1400 (c) Contraction (myosin heads); active transport of Ca²⁺; protein synthesis; glycogen synthesis.

items.stem: Scientists in Dhaka are studying how β cells of the pancreas make insulin. (a) Explain what happens to the primary transcript before it leaves the nucleus. (b) Explain why the same mRNA can be translated by many ribosomes at once, and why this is useful. (c) Suggest why β cells of the pancreas contain large amounts of RER and many ribosomes.
items.answer: (a) Introns are removed (spliced out) and exons joined to form mature mRNA. (b) Ribosomes move along mRNA, so others can attach behind (polysome); many copies of the protein made quickly. (c) Insulin is a protein made in large amounts (for secretion / function); ribosomes are the site of translation; RER transports protein to Golgi.

items.stem: In some regions of West Africa, about 30% of people carry the sickle cell allele, HbS. The mutation is a single base substitution in the gene for the β-globin polypeptide, changing codon 6 of the mRNA from GAG (glutamic acid) to GUG (valine). (a) State the DNA template strand triplets for the normal and mutant codons. (b) Explain how the change in one amino acid affects the haemoglobin molecule. (c) Describe two symptoms of sickle cell anaemia.
items.answer: (a) Normal CTC; mutant CAC. (b) Valine is non-polar / hydrophobic, unlike charged glutamic acid; at low oxygen it causes HbS molecules to stick together, forming long fibres that distort the red blood cell. (c) Anaemia / tiredness (less oxygen carried); pain and organ damage from blocked capillaries.
